Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help deter- mine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate’s 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement. 1 I NTRODUCTION Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has attracted growing interest for its potential to enhance agents’ capabilities without retraining their underlying language models (Ren et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Offline methods can learn from completed trajectories, but deploy one shared harness for the task agent that may arXiv:2611.05139v1 [cs.AI] 3 Nov 2026 overfits training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online evolution can adapt before, during or after one run through an evolver, but may have to reason about every intervention from scratch, or rely on verifier feedback which is usually unavailable at test-time. We introduce Meta2 , which moves offline optimization one level up: rather than optimizing a shared harness, it learns reusable knowledge for harness evolution and applies it within each task online. Offline, Meta2 learns a textual Meta-Skill ℳ by contrasting training rollouts of the same task agent under three configurations: without an evolver, with an evolver guided by the current version of ℳ, and with an evolver given privileged verifier information available only during training. Contrasts in trajectories and outcomes are aggregated across tasks to refine ℳ into reusable guidance on when and how to evolve, when to leave the harness unchanged, and which interventions to avoid. Online, an evolver combines the frozen ℳ with emerging trajectory evidence to decide whether to KEEP the harness unchanged or EVOLVE it through a task-local edit. Each edit shapes the … dits task-local. Project: https://meta-square.github.io/ 1. Introduction Long-horizon agents do not act through a model alone. They act through a harness: prompts that frame decisions, a context policy that preserves information, tools and hooks that enable actions, and checks for completion [26, 35, 45, 51]. These mechanisms are often fixed before execution, yet the need to adapt them emerges during execution. A missing tool becomes apparent when the agent tries to use it; an overlooked constraint may surface in an intermediate artifact; and a one-time warning may need to become a recurring check. A harness chosen in advance must anticipate such situations before the trajectory that exposes them exists. Because different tasks expose different interface and control needs, hand-designed harnesses [3, 5, 36, 49] must either anticipate a wide range of situations or be specialized manually. Automatic harness optimization reduces this burden, but most methods still make their consequential choices outside the active run. Offline methods optimize prompts, memory, tools, workflows, or complete harness programs on training tasks and deploy one shared artifact [1, 20, 24, 50, 54, 56, 58, 60]. This shared artifact may overfit training tasks and cannot react to evidence revealed during a new run. Online methods adapt the harness after the target task becomes available. Some customize it from the target instruction before execution (pre-run) or revise it using feedback from completed attempts (after-run) [39, 43, 57]. Recent systems support within-run evolution by updating prompts, tools, skills, or memory during execution [6, 18, 46, 47]. papers.title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
papers.first_page: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists Yuxuan Du,1, 2, ∗ Hanqing Zhao,1, ∗ Xinbiao Wang,1 Yiming Lu,1 Kaining Zhang,1 and Dacheng Tao1, † 1 College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 639798, Singapore 2 School of Physical and Mathematical Sciences, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore 639798, Singapore AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in com- putational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into exe- cutable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists arXiv:2611.02833v1 [quant-ph] 2 Nov 2026 often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally veri- fied workflow repairs i … der realistic resource constraints, requiring careful co-design of algorithms and hardware capabilities [21–24]. For quantum property characterization, extracting infor- mative properties from limited measurements becomes difficult as the Hilbert space grows exponentially, motivating efficient measurement and inference protocols [25–30]. As a result, these challenges create an urgent need for more autonomous approaches to computational quantum science. Recent breakthroughs in AI scientists offer a potential route towards autonomous computational quantum sci- ence [31–33]. By integrating frontier large language models (LLMs) with planning, tool use and iterative feedback [34–37], these systems have begun to automate algorithm discovery in mathematics [38–40] and software engineer- ing [41–44]. This trend is also extending to other disciplines, such as biology [45–47], chemistry [48–50] and materials science [51]. All of these advances point to a shift from AI-assisted research towards autonomous algorithm discovery. Computational quantum science is a natural next arena because progress in this field may reshape both what we can learn from quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. In this context, early efforts have demonstrated AI-driven discovery of quantum error-correcting codes [52–54], automated design of quantum circuits [55–57] and algorithmic search for quantum-chemistry applications [58–61]. However, the progress remains fragmented and largely confined to narrowly defined settings, such as a single subproblem, a human-tailored workflow or a search space strongly constrained by prior knowledge. papers.title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?
papers.first_page: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks? Jeremy Qin1,2∗ Ruizhi Deng1 Mohamed Osama Ahmed1 Frederick Tung1 Leo Feng1 1 RBC Borealis 2 ELLIS Institute Tübingen, arXiv:2611.05108v1 [cs.AI] 3 Nov 2026 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen AI Center Abstract Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce C ONTINUAL AUTO R ESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities. 1 Introduction Recently, there has been a growing interest in scaling frontier language models to different AI R&D processes [Huang et al., 2024, Lu et al., 2026]. From optimizing a set of hyperparameters to post- training small language models, agents are becoming more autonomous, and more capable of tackling complex and lengthy tasks [Karpathy, 2026, Rank et al., 2026]. As these agents shift towards longer horizon tasks, they increasingly accumulate insights, strategies, and practical experience. In real- world research, scientists often carry lessons from one project to the next, whether by reusing code or reapplying a specific post-training algorithm for example. We ask the question of whether experience acquired from one problem can benefit subsequent ones. Answering this requires understanding whether agents can retain knowledge across tasks and use it to adapt more effectively to new ones, bridging continual learning and meta-learning [Zhao et al., 2024, Asawa et al., 2026, Shu et al., 2026]. We study this setting without updating model weights, in which case experience is transferred only through the state accumulated during execution. Existing evaluations treat each R&D problem in isolation by resetting the agent from scratch before each new task. Although autoresearch-style loops allow agents to use feedback to optimize solutions iteratively, the acquired experience is discarded once the task is finished. Consequently, these evaluations cannot assess if lessons about experimental design, modeling choices, or execution failures can be applied to related tasks and improve future research. papers.first_page: Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents Taiming Lu1 Qi Xu2 Zhigang Hua2 Zhuang Liu1 1 Princeton University 2 Meta Abstract arXiv:2611.03618v1 [cs.AI] 2 Nov 2026 A model is only half of an AI agent system. The other half is the inference strategy: the reasoning procedure that turns model calls into a response. Today that second half is written by hand, and the experience of building one strategy never carries to the next. We introduce Strategist, a meta-agent that evolves inference strategies across tasks. Each strategy is written as a blueprint, executable code that other strategies can reuse, and together the blueprints form a library. Given a task and a small development set, Strategist retrieves related blueprints, writes candidate strategies, tests them on real samples, and revises them from the results. Every candidate then enters the library, so later tasks build on earlier discoveries. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist beats the strongest baseline on 24 and matches its average accuracy (74.7% vs. 74.0%) at 39% lower inference cost. Its strategies also transfer to unseen tasks and other models without further search. The part of an AI system that is not improved on its own now does. Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement Wenbo Huang1 Jianxin Bi1,2 Shunyu Yang1 Ruiyang Si1 Rui Ni1 Qiang Wang1 Shulong Jiang1 Yintianrun Zhang1 Feixiang Ruan1 Kewei Zhang1 Ye Huang1 Shukai Gong1 Daquan Zhou1,∗ 1 Peking University, 2 National University of Singapore arXiv:2611.08318v1 [cs.AI] 5 Nov 2026 ∗ Corresponding author Abstract Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark’s success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark’s criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs. papers.title: No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?
papers.first_page: SII-GAIR No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training? SII & Xinxu AI Abstract Pre-training is where every foundation model begins; bringing recursive self-improvement (RSI) there would let AI improve the process that creates AI, and could change how the entire industry builds foundation models. Yet public RSI work has so far targeted only post-training, which starts from an existing base model, runs trials costing GPU-hours, and returns verifiable scores. RSI for pre-training breaks all three conditions at orders- of-magnitude higher cost: a run consumes hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours over months and cannot be arXiv:2611.10719v1 [cs.AI] 7 Nov 2026 repeated; its objective, post-training headroom, cannot be read off any single score; and what must improve is not a model but the whole production & organization system, from data pipelines and training infrastructure to the teams that run them. To our knowledge, we are the first in the world to apply RSI to an entire frontier pre-training run from scratch, and to report it in detail. RSI does not stop at frontier pre-training, but it changes form: since no end-to-end loop can close over a single unrepeatable run, we decompose the pre-training loop into smaller loops that can, each repairing a step the full run breaks. The result is 801-30B-A3B-Base, a 30B-A3B MoE model trained from scratch on 11.8T tokens in three months by a newly formed team. We release it as a base model: full post-training is left to a subsequent release, and the lightweight SFT reported here (6B tokens, no RL) only probes post-training headroom. As a base model, 801-30B-A3B outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and keeps this position under identical SFT; with lightweight SFT alone, it achieves the highest average on four agentic benchmarks against fully post-trained models, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Post-training RSI starts where this work ends: it presupposes a strong base model, exactly what pre-training must produce. Yet harness design remains largely manual, and automating it requires navigating an open-ended search space through costly end-to-end evaluations. We introduce H ARNESS F LOW, a framework for optimizing complete executable har- nesses under a limited candidate-evaluation budget, with the model and task en- vironment held fixed. H ARNESS F LOW organizes candidates and their evaluation histories in a refinement tree, using a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based policy to balance exploitation and exploration. A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable har- ness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, H ARNESS F LOW achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six bench- marks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized har- nesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incur- ring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward au- tomating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents. 1 I NTRODUCTION The performance of LLM agents depends not only on the underlying model but also on the har- ness, the executable system that governs access to information, maintains state, invokes tools, and coordinates execution (Yang et al., 2024b; Shang et al., 2025; Khattab et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025). Prior studies of context management and multi-agent systems show that these mechanisms can sub- stantially affect agent behavior (Packer et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023), highlighting harness design as a practical means of improving agent performance without modifying model weights. However, harness design remains largely manual and expertise-intensive, making effective designs difficult to adapt and reuse across tasks and domains (Zhang et al., 2025b). Recent work has sought to automate harness design and refinement to reduce reliance on manual engineering (Zhuge et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; 2025a; Yue et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2026). Meta-Harness (Lee et al., 2026) permits full-harness code refinement, while AutoSaddler (Park et al., 2026) organizes durable updates from agent execution traces. DarwinX (Zhang et al., 2026d) explores harness pop- ulations through selection and preservation checks. papers.first_page: REINS: A Self-Evolving Agent Harness for Real-Time Trajectory Planning Zhihong Cui1∗ Hengyu Liu2∗† Haoran Tang3 Shijun Liu4 Amir Taherkordi1 Tor Skeie1,5 1 Department of Informatics, University of Oslo, Norway 2 Department of Computer Science, Aalborg University, Denmark arXiv:2611.10748v1 [cs.RO] 7 Nov 2026 3 Department of Computing, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong SAR, China 4 Shandong Key Laboratory of Foundational Software, School of Software, Shandong University, China 5 Simula Research Laboratory, Norway Abstract Agent harnesses—runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM’s reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory—have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision—leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM–planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9–4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. A demonstration-aware gate admits skills based on student mastery or sufficient successful teacher demonstrations. The student learns from selected action traces with context from an Engram Trace Graph (ETG). Release requires valid training participation and scores meeting both relative and absolute criteria; records for skills that fail verification remain retrievable. papers.first_page: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities Haoyang Zhang† Qumeng Sun Xiao Zhang Xiang Liu Zhidong Fan Junjie Wang arXiv:2611.07595v1 [cs.SE] 5 Nov 2026 Infinite Evolution Lab, EvoMap https://github.com/EvoMap/evolver Abstract Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this ex- perience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experi- ence acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience- conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four bench- marks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. papers.title: When Experience Becomes a Backdoor: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Failure-Aware Task Optimization
papers.first_page: When Experience Becomes a Backdoor: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Failure-Aware Task Optimization Minhua Lin1 , Zongyu Wu1 , Hanqing Lu3 , Xianfeng Tang2 , Xiang Zhang1 , Qi He2 , Suhang Wang1 1 The Pennsylvania State University, 2 Microsoft, 3 Independent Researcher Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly improve themselves through self-evolution, distilling execution experience into persistent, reusable skills. However, this persistence creates a new attack arXiv:2611.10542v1 [cs.CR] 7 Nov 2026 surface: malicious rules implanted into skills can compromise subsequent agent behavior. Existing skill backdoor attacks typically assume direct manipulation of the victim’s skills, which is impractical when skills are constructed internally by a trusted evolver. In this paper, we study a novel problem of task-level backdoor attacks, where the attacker can only inject poisoned evolution tasks, inducing the agent to implant backdoors into its own skills. Since the attacker controls neither skill induction nor downstream execution, a natural approach is to iteratively optimize poisoned tasks based on attack success. However, our preliminary analysis reveals two key challenges: (i) failures at different stages of skill evolution and downstream execution can produce indistinguishable outcomes, providing little guidance for targeted poisoned-task updates; and (ii) unsuccessful updates may undermine earlier progress, while simply discarding them may lead to repeated ineffective updates. To address these challenges, we propose BadEvolve, a failure-aware task-poisoning framework against self-evolving LLM agents. BadEvolve diagnoses attack failures across four stages, i.e., Induction, Activation, Following, and Effect, and directs updates toward the failing stage. It further employs rollback to preserve earlier progress and failure memory to avoid repeating ineffective updates. Extensive experiments across diverse self-evolution frameworks, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of BadEvolve. Correspondence: mfl5681@psu.edu, szw494@psu.edu Code: https://github.com/ventr1c/BadEvolve 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) [28, 29, 36] agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks such as web interaction [54] and software engineering [10] by interacting with external environments. In these settings, the agent’s behavior depends not only on the underlying model but also on its harness, including prompts [42], skills [13], memories [44], and tools [27], which shapes how the model observes, reasons, acts, and recovers from errors. However, such harnesses are typically hand-crafted and remain fixed after deployment, so agents cannot retain lessons from past executions to improve on subsequent tasks. To address this limitation, self-evolution has emerged as a promising paradigm for LLM agents [8, 17], enabling them to update their harness based on execution experience so that lessons from past tasks can inform future behavior. Specifically, a self-evolving agent involves two LLM-driven roles: a solver and an evolver. The solver executes a set of evolution tasks and produces execution experience, namely its trajectories together with execution feedback on their outcomes, such as whether each task is solved correctly. The evolver then analyzes this experience to identify what led to success or failure, and distills the resulting lessons into updates to the harness, which the solver reuses on future tasks [19, 33, 41, 53]. In particular, skill-based self-evolution [24, 30, 38] has attracted growing attention: rather than storing raw interaction records, it organizes these lessons into modular, reusable skills that encode procedural knowledge, enabling them to transfer across tasks. 1
